A slide says: "Sculley and colleagues showed that less than 10% of the code
in a production ML system is the model." The link they cite returns HTTP

What does the paper actually say?

insists on two separate checks, and the second is the one people skip: the
URL resolves, *and* the page contains the claim you are citing it for. A
200 is evidence of the first only. The underlying point survives without
the number, which is exactly why the number was never needed.

items.context:
Public Health England, September 2020. Test results were consolidated into
Excel templates in the legacy `.xls` format, which caps a worksheet at
65,536 rows.

What happened when a file hit the ceiling?
items.why:
15,841 positive cases went unreported for a week, and the contacts of those
people were not traced. No exception, no alert, no partial record to
notice: the failure mode was silence. This is the course's opening argument
in one incident. The model was not the problem, there was no model; the
problem was a data pipeline with a capacity limit and no check that what
went in came out.
items.true: The remaining rows were not rejected with an error; they were simply absent
false: The import failed with an error, and the backlog was reprocessed once the format was changed
The file was split automatically, and the second part was processed a day late
The rows were truncated to fit, so partial records entered the system

items.context:
Google Flu Trends screened 50 million candidate queries down to 45 and
reported a mean correlation of 0.97 across nine regions, on held-out data
excluded from every prior modeling step.

Before you look: was the validation protocol the problem?
items.why:
This is the uncomfortable one, and it is why the case is in the notes.
Held-out validation was done properly and the system still degraded, because
the world changed underneath it: search behavior was not a stable proxy for
influenza, and the relationship the model learned did not survive. Validating
well is not evidence that a system works. It is evidence that it worked on
data you already had.
items.true: No. The protocol was more disciplined than a great deal of deployed machine learning gets, and it still failed in production
false: Yes; screening 50 million candidates guarantees spurious correlations survive to the held-out set
Yes; nine regions is too few to support a correlation estimate
No, and the failure was purely an infrastructure outage rather than a modeling issue

items.context:
Engineering data differs from the datasets in a general ML tutorial in a way
that changes what you have to build. What is the difference?
items.why:
Size and noise are real and neither is the distinguishing property. What
makes engineering data different is that somebody may later have to
establish which instrument produced a number, when it was calibrated, and
what the model recommended on the basis of it. That is a requirement about
records rather than about accuracy, and no amount of model quality
substitutes for it.
items.true: It carries provenance and traceability requirements, because the outputs feed decisions with physical and safety consequences
false: It is larger, so the tooling has to scale further than a tutorial's does
It is noisier, so more of the effort goes into cleaning than into modeling
It is proprietary, so it cannot be shared and every project starts from scratch

items.context:
The 737 MAX case is often summarized as "the software was buggy."

What do the investigations say about the sensor architecture?
items.why:
The generalisable shape is not about aircraft. A system that acts on one
input has no way to notice that the input is wrong, so the failure is in the
architecture rather than in the code that ran correctly on bad data. Ask of
your own systems what a single wrong sensor reading would do, and whether
anything downstream could tell.
items.true: That the system acted on a single angle-of-attack sensor, so one faulty input had no contradiction available
false: That redundant sensors were fitted and the voting logic failed to use them
That the sensors were correct and the fault lay entirely in pilot training
That sensor data was corrupted in transit between the vane and the flight computer

items.context:
The course standardizes on `uv` for environments. What failure is that

items.context:
Open [`l01-reproducibility.ipynb`](../lectures/l01/l01-reproducibility.ipynb)
and run it top to bottom. It is deliberately defective.

One cell fails for you and a different one fails for your neighbor. Why?
items.why:
`np.trapz` was removed in NumPy 2.0 and `np.trapezoid` was added there, so
exactly one cell fails whichever version you installed, and comparing
failures with a neighbor is the discussion. The absolute path is one of
the other two deliberate defects and it fails for everybody, which is why it
is the less interesting one: a defect that only fires on some machines is
the kind that reaches production.
items.true: It integrates a curve twice, once with `np.trapz` and once with `np.trapezoid`, and exactly one exists in your NumPy version
false: Random seeds differ between machines, so the split is different
The absolute path only exists on the author's machine, so everyone fails identically there
Cell execution order differs, so the failure depends on how you ran it

items.context:
Your model's accuracy is unchanged on the test set, but users report it has
got worse over the last quarter.

What is the most likely explanation, and where does the response belong?
items.why:
This is Google Flu Trends in miniature, and it is why "validating well is
not evidence that a system works" is a section heading rather than an
aside. A frozen test set is exactly right for comparing versions and tells
you nothing about whether the world it was drawn from still exists. L23
turns this into instrumentation.
items.true: The world moved and the frozen test set did not, so the response is monitoring the input distribution rather than re-scoring the same data
false: The users are wrong; a stable test score means stable behavior
The model has degraded numerically, so retraining on the same data will restore it
The test set has leaked into training, which inflates the score while real performance falls

items.context:
"We locked the environment, pinned the seed, and tracked the run, so the
result is trustworthy."

What does that argument miss?
items.why:
Reproducibility makes a result *checkable*; it is a precondition for
catching errors, not a substitute for doing so. Note how the Duke errors
were actually caught: not by re-running the original code, which would have
reproduced its mistakes, but by outside statisticians re-implementing the
analysis from scratch and finding the two disagreed. Reproduction confirms
you can regenerate a number. Confirming it is right is a separate act
called validation.
items.true: Reproducible is not the same as correct: a pipeline with an off-by-one error will reproduce the wrong answer with perfect fidelity
false: Nothing, provided the lockfile is regenerated whenever a dependency changes
Seeds do not make a result reproducible across platforms, so the claim overstates what pinning buys
Tracking is only meaningful if the tracked run is also deployed, which this does not say

items.context:
A lockfile pins the exact version of every Python package. What does it
still not pin?
items.why:
A package version is not the same as the code that runs. The lockfile says
nothing about system C libraries, the CUDA toolkit, or the operating system,
and a pinned version can even become unavailable if it is removed from the
index. For most engineering work that is enough; when you need the whole
stack frozen the tool is a container, which is a Week 12 topic. The honest
framing is that `uv` gives you a reproducible Python environment, which is
most of what you need and not quite all of it.
items.true: The compiled bytes: platform-specific wheels differ between macOS and Linux, and system C libraries are not covered at all
false: The random seed, which has to be set separately in code
Transitive dependencies, which resolve freshly on each install
The Python interpreter version, which is recorded separately

sequence.prompt: The uv commands of a normal day, in the order you reach for them.
sequence.why: init creates the project, add resolves and locks a dependency, run executes inside the environment after checking the lockfile still matches pyproject.toml, and sync rebuilds the whole thing from the lockfile on a machine that has never seen it. The last one is the one that ends "works on my machine".

items.context:
Twenty minutes of poking at a file to decide whether an idea is worth
pursuing. Should you set up a locked, tracked, packaged project first?
items.why:
There is a real judgment call about when to pay for the discipline. Full
scaffolding on a twenty-minute exploration is cumbersome and is its own kind
of over-engineering. The moment an analysis will be rerun, shared, built
upon, or believed by anyone, including your future self, it has crossed the
line, and almost nobody notices the crossing at the time. So the default
leans toward scaffolding, because retrofitting is the expensive direction.
items.true: No for a genuinely throwaway exploration, but the trap is that results cross the line into needing it quietly
false: Yes, always; the discipline is cheap and retrofitting is expensive
No; scaffolding is only warranted once a result is going to be published
Yes, because an unlocked environment cannot produce a result worth acting on at all

items.context:
A content hash tells you two runs used different data. What does it not
tell you?
items.why:
A hash is a smoke alarm, not an investigation. Detecting change is the
floor of data provenance rather than the ceiling, and the tools that go
further, versioning data by content with a readable history of what changed
and why, are `git-lfs` and DVC. Collisions are not the concern: the hash is
certain that the file differs, and useless about everything after that.
items.true: Which rows changed, whether the change was a fix or a corruption, or whether it matters
false: Whether the file is genuinely different, since hashes collide in practice
When the change happened, which requires a timestamp alongside the hash
Who made the change, which requires an audit log rather than a hash

items.context:
Every run in your MLflow project logs a seed. A colleague concludes the
project is reproducible.

What is wrong with that inference?
items.why:
The tracker is a filing system, and a filing system is only as trustworthy
as the discipline of the person filing. Logging a seed documents one input
to a run that may still be irreproducible for a dozen other reasons. The
third option is a real and separate concern; it is not the flaw in the
inference, which is that recording is being mistaken for guaranteeing.
items.true: Tracking records, it does not enforce: MLflow will faithfully log a run whose environment was never locked
false: Nothing; a logged seed plus logged parameters is what reproducibility means in practice
Seeds are per-library, so one logged seed does not cover NumPy, PyTorch and Python's own RNG
The seed should be logged as a tag rather than a parameter, or it will not be searchable

items.context: Why do large binary files not belong in plain git?
items.why:
Code, data, and models are three different versioning problems and the
session is explicit that one tool does not serve all three. Git is superb
for text it can diff and terrible for a 400 MB file rewritten weekly,
because every version stays in the history forever. That the diffs are
uninformative is true and is not the binding cost; the binding cost is that
the repository stops being clonable.
items.true: Git stores a full copy of every version, so a repeatedly-changed binary makes the history unusable to clone
false: Git rejects files above a fixed size limit, so they cannot be committed at all
Git cannot compute diffs for binary content, so the commits carry no information
Binary files break the working tree on checkout across operating systems

items.context:
What is the point of turning an exploratory notebook into a module with a
command-line entry point?
items.why:
Notebooks are version-controllable, awkwardly, so that is not the argument.
The argument is that a notebook's execution order is a human decision made
at runtime, and a module's is not. Once there is an entry point, CI can run
it, a scheduler can run it, and a test can assert what it produces, none of
which is available to a sequence of cells.
items.true: It becomes testable and callable, so the thing you validated can be run again by something other than a human clicking cells
false: Speed, since a script runs faster than the same code in a notebook kernel
Notebooks cannot be version-controlled, so moving to a script is what makes the work reviewable
It reduces memory use, since a script releases state between stages

sequence.prompt: The notebook refactor: the functions the data moves through, in order.
sequence.why: The refactor is mechanical, which is the good news. Each function takes its inputs as arguments and returns a value, so it can be imported and tested on its own rather than depending on the ambient state of a notebook that has to be run in an order you remember.

only found when outside statisticians built the analysis again from scratch
and the two versions disagreed.

false: Comparing lockfiles, since a dependency difference is the likeliest cause of a numeric disagreement

What does `uv` produce that a `requirements.txt` does not?
items.why:
A requirements file is a request; a lockfile is a record. The distinction
only bites when a transitive dependency moves under you, which is exactly
the failure L13 documents when scikit-learn 1.8 and 1.9 assigned folds
differently under an identical call. Speed is real and is not the reason
this is in the toolchain.
items.true: A lockfile recording what was actually installed, including transitive dependencies, rather than what was asked for
false: A faster install, since uv resolves dependencies in parallel
A virtual environment, which requirements.txt cannot create
A dependency graph, which requirements.txt flattens and loses

items.context:
```sql
SELECT * FROM readings WHERE value <> 30;
```
Your sensor table has nulls in `value`. What does this return?
items.why:
SQL has three truth values, not two: true, false, and unknown. "Unknown is
not equal to 30" evaluates to unknown rather than to true, so the row is
not returned. This is defined semantics rather than a defect, and it
quietly produces wrong analyses for anyone who forgets it. The same family
contains a worse one: `NOT IN` against a subquery containing a single null
returns no rows at all.
items.true: Every row whose value is not 30, silently excluding all null rows
false: Every row whose value is not 30, including the null ones, since null is not 30
An error, since a comparison against null is not permitted in a WHERE clause
Every row, since null comparisons default to true in PostgreSQL

items.context:
A mote dropped half its readings. You compute `avg(value)` over its rows.
What do you get?
items.why:
`count(*)` counts rows while `count(value)` counts only non-null ones, and
`avg(value)` averages only the readings that are present. So the mote is
not penalized in the average unless you have separately counted how many it
reported. The habit worth forming is to carry a completeness count next to
any aggregate over sensor data, because the aggregate alone cannot tell you
whether it summarizes everything or half of it.
items.true: An average over the readings that are present, with the missing ones simply absent from it
false: An average that treats missing readings as zero, biasing it downward
Null, because any aggregate over a column containing nulls is null
An error, unless the nulls are filtered out first

items.context:
Your experiment metadata records a different, unpredictable set of fields
for every run. You are putting it in PostgreSQL and the schema keeps
changing.

What does that tell you?
items.why:
The same schema that protected your readings table is expensive to change
once it is large, and a migration against a nine-million-row table in a live
deployment is a real operation with real risk. Heterogeneous metadata is the
case where rigidity stops paying, and recognizing it is the point: the
relational model is a default, not a universal answer. A JSON column is a
genuine option and it is the relational model conceding the argument rather
than winning it.
items.true: That this is exactly the territory where the rigid schema stops helping and document stores earn their place
false: That the schema needs a JSON column, which restores flexibility inside the relational model
That the runs should be normalized further, into a table per field type
That migrations should be automated, since the schema churn is a tooling problem

items.context:
Why store sensor data long (one row per reading) rather than wide (one
column per sensor)?
items.why:
A wide table encodes your current instrument list into the schema, so
commissioning a sensor becomes a migration and decommissioning one leaves a
column of nulls forever. Long tables decouple the two. The cost is real and
worth knowing: queries that want several channels side by side now need a
pivot or a join, which is why the session spends time on window functions
and time bucketing.
items.true: Adding a sensor is a new row rather than a schema change, and the schema stops depending on which instruments exist
false: Long tables compress better, so the storage cost is lower at scale
Long tables are faster to query, since the index fits in memory
Wide tables cannot represent timestamps consistently across sensors

items.context:
"We used a timestamp column, so the times are correct."

What did 30 June 2012 demonstrate?
items.why:
The case is in the notes because a type that carries physical meaning has
to cope with how the physical quantity actually behaves, and time is the one
everybody assumes is simple. Timezones are a real hazard and a different
one. The general shape is the session's argument about types: a column
declared with the right type is carrying a claim about the world, and the
world occasionally declines to cooperate.
items.true: That a leap second is a real event a timestamp type has to survive, and systems assuming fixed-length days failed
false: That timezone conversion is the main hazard, and UTC storage solves it
That NTP drift accumulates faster than most systems account for
That millisecond precision is insufficient for high-rate sensor data

items.context:
When should a measured quantity be stored as `numeric` rather than
`double precision`?
items.why:
"Always" is the tempting answer and it is wrong: `numeric` is materially
slower and most sensor readings are approximate measurements of a
continuous quantity, where double precision is the honest representation.
The session is also blunt that this does not save you from floating point
elsewhere: a value read into Python as a float is a float again, whatever
the column said.
items.true: When exactness at the stored precision matters more than arithmetic speed, for instance for money or a regulated tolerance
false: Always, since numeric is exact and double precision is approximate
When the values span many orders of magnitude, which double precision handles poorly
Never for sensor data, since numeric cannot represent scientific notation

items.context:
A column is declared `double precision NOT NULL`. A reading arrives as
-9999, the instrument's error sentinel.

What happens?
items.why:
The type says "this is a number that is present". It says nothing about
whether the number is physically possible. Sentinels like -9999 are
extremely common in instrument data and they pass every type check, which
is why the session insists on `CHECK` constraints for range and on
validation as a separate layer. This is the same lesson as the units
assertion in L7: the declaration is not the check.
items.true: It is stored, because a typed column is still not a validated column
false: The insert is rejected, since -9999 is outside any plausible physical range
It is coerced to null, since the sentinel is recognized by the driver
It is stored and flagged, since PostgreSQL tracks out-of-range values

sequence.prompt: Loading a sensor export that resists the loader, through a staging table.

insert into the real readings table

Some of them you do not have to write at all: the foreign key to sensors rejects the corrupt mote ids for you the moment you try to insert one.

items.context:
A time-range query over a large readings table is slow. You add an index
and it is still slow.

What tells you why?
items.why:
Every other option is a real diagnostic and each answers a narrower
question. The plan is the one that tells you what the database actually
decided to do, which is frequently not what you assumed when you added the
index: a predicate that wraps the column in a function, or a range broad
enough that a sequential scan is genuinely cheaper, both produce a
correctly-ignored index.
items.true: The query plan, from `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, which shows whether the index was used and what it cost
false: The table statistics, which show whether the index is selective enough to help
The query duration across repeated runs, which distinguishes cold cache from a bad plan
The index size on disk, which indicates whether it fits in memory

items.context:
Open [`l03-sql-timeseries.ipynb`](../lectures/l03/l03-sql-timeseries.ipynb)
and run the same range query with and without the index, reading the plan
each time.

What changes in the plan?
items.why:
An index that exists and an index that is used are different things, and
the plan is the only place the difference is visible. This is the same
discipline as the rest of the course: the artifact exists is not the same
claim as the artifact works, and you check by looking at what actually
happened rather than at what you configured.
items.true: The scan type changes, and the plan shows whether the index was actually chosen rather than merely present
false: Only the timing; the plan is identical because the planner is deterministic
The row estimates change, since an index updates the table statistics
Nothing visible; index use is reported only in the server log

items.context:
Records in your system are constantly corrected one at a time. Someone
proposes storing them as Parquet for the analytics speedup.

What is wrong with that?
items.why:
The layout that makes analytical scans fast makes changes slow. Column
stores lose the point write, and that is a property to respect rather than
a defect to engineer around: data that is constantly corrected belongs in
the row store from L3. Batching helps and does not change the shape of the
argument, which is about matching the store to the access pattern.
items.true: A Parquet file is effectively immutable: there is no in-place update, so a single correction rewrites the file that holds it
false: Nothing, provided the corrections are batched nightly rather than applied individually
Parquet cannot represent the schema changes that corrections imply
Parquet loses precision on repeated rewrites, so corrections accumulate error

items.context:
"After that lecture, we should replace PostgreSQL with DuckDB and Parquet."

What is wrong with this conclusion?
items.why:
PostgreSQL absorbs the live writes with its schema and transactions intact,
and the history is periodically written out as Parquet that DuckDB scans.
The skill is not loyalty to a column store or a row store; it is placing each
part of the workload where its access pattern is cheap, and moving data
across the seam deliberately.
items.true: It is named in the notes as the most common mistake after the lecture: the two compose, and a real platform runs both
false: Nothing; for analytical workloads the replacement is the recommended migration
DuckDB cannot read PostgreSQL, so the migration would lose the existing data
Parquet lacks the type system to represent what a relational schema encodes

items.context: What is DuckDB not?
items.why:
DuckDB runs inside one process, which is both its convenience and its
boundary: superb for one analyst's laptop, one pipeline's transform step,
one service's embedded analytics, and not trying to be a concurrent
multi-writer server. When several writers need a single consistent view,
that is the relational server's job, and DuckDB complements it rather than
trying to replace it.
items.true: A shared transactional backend that many clients write to concurrently with isolation guarantees
false: An analytical engine, since it is optimized for point lookups rather than scans
A SQL engine, since it uses its own dialect rather than standard SQL
Usable without a server, since it requires a background process to hold state

items.context:
Columnar storage gives a large measured speedup on analytical scans.

Before you look: at what data size does that advantage appear?
items.why:
The measured 80-times speedup appears at millions of rows. Below that scale
a pandas `groupby` is simpler, fast enough, and one fewer moving part, and
reaching for the columnar machinery is over-engineering, the same lesson L2
made about scaffolding a throwaway script. Match the tool to the size as
well as to the access pattern.
items.true: At millions of rows; it shrinks at a few hundred thousand and vanishes on data that fits in memory
false: At a few thousand rows, since the layout advantage is structural rather than a matter of scale
Only above a billion rows, below which the formats are indistinguishable
At any size, though the factor grows with row count

items.context: Why does a column store accelerate an analytical scan?
items.why:
Compression is a genuine second-order benefit and it follows from the same
property: values in a column are homogeneous, so they compress far better
than a row of mixed types. But the primary mechanism is that the layout
lets you skip what you did not ask for, and that is why the advantage is
about access pattern rather than about size alone.
items.true: A query touching three of forty columns reads only those three, instead of every row in full
false: It compresses better, so less data has to be read from disk overall
It keeps an index on every column, so any predicate can be answered from an index
It stores data pre-aggregated, so common groupings are already computed

items.context:
A colleague wants a document store because designing the schema is taking
too long.

Is that a good reason?
items.why:
Document, key-value, and time-series stores each solve a real problem by
giving something up, and what they give up is usually the relational
contract from L3: the enforced schema, the joins, the transactions. That is
the right trade when the data genuinely does not fit a table, and a bad one
when it is a way of not deciding. The fourth option is wrong in a different
direction: they are not slower everywhere, they are faster at the pattern
they were built for.
items.true: No. Choose one because your access pattern demands it, not because a schema felt like work
false: Yes; schema design is a bottleneck and document stores let it be deferred until the shape settles
Yes, provided a schema is imposed later at the application layer
No, because document stores are slower than relational databases at every access pattern

items.context: Which store fits "continuous writes, point lookups, strong consistency"?
items.why:
The rule the whole arc is building toward: store data in the shape that
matches how it will be read. Continuous writes, point lookups and strong
consistency say row store; wide scans and aggregates over history say
column store. A document store does point lookups well and gives up the
consistency guarantee, which is exactly the part this question specified.
items.true: A row store and OLTP, which is the relational database of L3
false: A column store with Parquet files, since the writes can be appended as new files
A document store, since point lookups by key are its core operation
A time-series database, since it is built for high-rate timestamped writes

items.context:
A pipeline writes one Parquet file per reading, as readings arrive.

What is wrong?

step and a corresponding error floor, and the floor is many orders of
magnitude above machine precision. Autodiff is not a better approximation
of the derivative, it is the derivative, computed by the chain rule on the
operations you actually performed. That is why it lands at 1.7e-18 and a
difference quotient cannot.

It is miscalibrated, because it ignores the inputs
It is sharp but not calibrated

items.context:
On the calibration mixes, the z-scores (y − μ)/σ of an ensemble have a mean square well
above 1. You rescale every σ by the factor that minimizes the negative log likelihood.
What happens to the intervals?
items.why:
The best factor is the root mean square of the calibration z-scores. A mean square above 1
means the errors are larger than the stated σ, so the model was overconfident and the
factor widens every interval.
items.true: They get wider, because the factor is above 1
false: They get narrower, because the factor is below 1
They stay the same width and shift toward the data
Nothing, because rescaling cannot change coverage

items.context:
With its kernel settings held fixed, what does a Gaussian process's predictive variance
depend on?
items.why:
The variance formula contains the kernel values between inputs and no y at all. At fixed
settings a GP that fits badly reports the same band as one that fits well; y reaches the
band only through fitted hyperparameters.
items.true: Only the inputs and the kernel, not the observed targets
false: The training targets, so a poor fit widens the band
The residuals of the mean on the training points
The number of points only, not where they are

items.context:
A team adds more simulation runs to an RBF Gaussian process and notices the fitted length
scale falls every time: 0.09, then 0.06, then 0.03. They conclude the model is resolving
finer detail. What did they miss?
items.true: A length scale that keeps shrinking signals a kernel that does not fit the function, such as a step
false: Nothing; a shorter length scale always means a better model
The optimizer is failing to converge as the data grow
The noise level is too high for an RBF kernel

items.context:
Why is a Gaussian process fitted to five points, with its settings chosen by maximum
likelihood, often overconfident?
items.why:
Short and long length scales fit five points about equally, and the uncertainty about which
is right never reaches the band. Over 200 data sets of five points, the median coverage of
a nominal 95% band was 78%.
items.true: Many settings explain five points equally well, and maximum likelihood keeps one as if known
false: Five points are too few to compute a posterior at all
Maximum likelihood always overestimates the noise
The band cannot widen beyond the data with so few points

items.context:
Noise in a data set grows with x. A Gaussian process with one noise level covers 95% over
the whole range. What does checking coverage by region show?
items.why:
One fitted noise level sits between the small and the large noise, so the band is too wide
on the quiet side and too narrow on the noisy side. By third of the range the toy problem
gave 100%, 98% and 88%.
items.true: Too wide where the noise is small, too narrow where it is large
false: 95% everywhere, since the overall number is right
Too narrow where the noise is small, too wide where it is large
Too narrow everywhere, hidden by rounding

items.context:
Ten networks trained from different seeds agree closely inside the training range, and a
95% interval built from their spread alone covers far less than 95% there. Why?
items.why:
Members disagree about the function, not about a new measurement. Inside the data they
agreed to 0.021 while the noise was 0.1, so the spread alone covered 29%; adding a noise
estimate brought it to 93%.
items.true: The spread measures only the epistemic part and leaves out the noise
false: The networks were not trained long enough
Ten members are too few for a stable spread
The spread is too large and overshoots the data

items.context: What does the spread of models refit on bootstrap resamples estimate?
items.why:
Resampling shows how the fit would change with a new data set of the same size. If every
resample makes the same mistake, the spread is small and the error large, so the bias is
missed, and so is the noise.
items.true: How much the fitted function varies with the data: the variance part of the error
false: The noise in a new measurement
The bias of the model, including its errors far from the data
The total prediction error, noise included

items.context:
An optimizer searches a surrogate for the strongest mix it can find, and the team reports
each proposed mix with a split conformal 90% interval, citing the method's finite-sample
guarantee. What is wrong?
items.why:
The guarantee needs only exchangeability, and an optimizer breaks it on purpose. On the
strongest mixes, held out because they differ, split conformal covered 56% at a nominal 90%.
items.true: Proposed mixes are chosen for being different, so they are not exchangeable with the calibration mixes
false: Split conformal needs Gaussian errors, which strengths are not
The calibration set must be larger than the training set
Conformal intervals cannot be used with neural networks

items.context: How does the width of a plain split conformal interval vary across inputs?
items.true: It is the same everywhere; the guarantee holds on average over inputs
false: It grows where the training data are sparse
It follows the noise level at each input
It shrinks as the model becomes more confident

items.context: What coverage does the jackknife+ guarantee for a target level of 1 − α?
items.why:
Barber et al. prove 1 − 2α and show the factor of 2 cannot be removed in general, while
reporting near 1 − α in practice. The plain jackknife has no guarantee, and its coverage can
vanish.
items.true: At least 1 − 2α in the worst case, and close to 1 − α in practice
false: Exactly 1 − α, like split conformal
At least 1 − α, but only with Gaussian errors
No guarantee at all, like the plain jackknife

items.context:
LinearRegressionUQ with a cubic basis, fitted to a sine on [0, 1], covers about 95% inside
the data and almost nothing beyond it, although its band widens there. Why?
items.why:
The parameter term says how unsure the coefficients of a cubic are, not whether a cubic is
the right shape. That is model inadequacy, and nothing inside the training range reveals it.
items.true: The cubic basis is wrong for a sine, and its uncertainty only covers fits within that basis
false: The noise estimate is too small
Linear regression cannot produce prediction intervals
The band widens too fast and overshoots

items.context:
While fitting, a pycse model prints "Model is well-calibrated", then covers well under 95%
beyond its training range. What did the message check?
items.why:
The validation points came from the same range as the training points, so the check is an
in-distribution statement. It says nothing about inputs beyond the data.
items.true: The rescaling factor on validation points from inside the training range
false: Coverage on a held-out region beyond the training data
That the network converged
That the residuals are Gaussian

items.context: What makes the reactor's yield a black-box objective?
items.why:
In the lab there is no formula and no gradient. You choose a temperature, run the
experiment for hours, and get one measured yield back, with noise. The kinetics formula in
the notes only plays the role of the lab.
items.true: You can only evaluate it: set the inputs, run it, read one noisy number
false: It comes from a neural network whose weights nobody can inspect or interpret
Its formula is known, but it is too long to differentiate by hand in the lab
It returns several outputs at once, so no single one of them can be optimized

items.context: Why is it called *Bayesian* optimization?
items.why:
The unknown is the whole function. A GP prior over it is updated by each experiment into a
posterior, and the next experiment is chosen on that posterior. Bayesian statistics for the
belief, plus a decision on it.
items.true: It updates a belief about the unknown curve with every experiment, and decides on that belief
false: It applies Bayes' rule to estimate the gradient of the yield from noisy finite differences
Its objective has to be a probability, such as a yield, so the method is named after Bayes
Thomas Bayes first used it to choose experiments, and the name stayed with the method

items.context:
You are fitting thousands of weights in a model whose loss and gradient take a millisecond to
compute. A colleague suggests Bayesian optimization. What do you answer?
items.why:
BO pays off when an evaluation is expensive, noisy and without gradients, with a budget of
tens and up to about 20 inputs. Cheap evaluations with gradients and many variables are
what gradient-based methods are built for.
items.true: Use a gradient-based method: evaluations are cheap, gradients exist, and there are too many inputs
false: Use BO: it searches globally, so it is always safer than a local gradient-based method
Use BO with a batch acquisition, so that it can run thousands of evaluations at once
Use random search: with that many weights, no surrogate model of the loss can help

items.context:
On the two-knob reactor, starting from the cold side, L-BFGS-B with finite-difference
gradients often stopped where it started. Why?
items.why:
A finite difference compares two noisy measurements. Where the true change is tiny, as on
the cold plateau, the difference is mostly noise, so the gradient points nowhere useful.
The surface has one optimum; the problem is the noise, not local optima.
items.true: Each gradient costs experiments, and the noise swamps the small differences on the flat cold side
false: The yield surface has many local optima, and L-BFGS-B was trapped in the nearest of them
L-BFGS-B needs exact second derivatives, which a noisy experiment can never provide
The temperature bounds stopped every step before it could get near the optimum

items.context: Which is one pass of the Bayesian optimization loop?
items.why:
Fit, score, run, add. The GP is refitted to every experiment so far on each pass, and the
next experiment is the maximizer of the acquisition function, not of the GP mean alone.
items.true: Fit the GP to all data, maximize the acquisition, run that experiment, add it to the data
false: Maximize the acquisition, fit the GP to the newest point only, run it, discard the older data
Run a batch of random experiments, fit the GP once, and report the maximum of its mean
Fit the GP, run the experiment where its mean is highest, then refit the acquisition function

items.context:
On the reactor, BO climbed from the cold side toward 80 °C, then experiment 8 jumped to
140 °C. What was that jump?
items.why:
The band was still wide at the hot end, so expected improvement there was not zero. That
experiment cost one run and collapsed the band; BO never went back there and settled at
80 °C.
items.true: Exploration: the GP was still unsure there, so expected improvement there was not zero
false: Exploitation: the GP mean predicted its highest yield of all at the hot end
A bug: expected improvement should never pick a point on the edge of the bounds
Chance: optimize_acqf returned one of its random candidates instead of the best

items.context: What goes wrong with pure exploitation?
items.why:
Exploitation goes where the mean is high, which is next to the incumbent. It never looks
elsewhere, so it cannot find a better region. Sampling where the band is widest is the
other extreme, pure exploration.
items.true: It keeps sampling next to the best point so far, and can sit on a local optimum forever
false: It samples wherever the band is widest, and spends the whole budget learning the curve
It needs the gradient of the objective, which a laboratory experiment cannot provide
It can only use the GP's standard deviation, and has to ignore the mean altogether

items.context: You raise κ in the upper confidence bound μ(x) + κσ(x). What changes in where it samples?
items.why:
κ multiplies σ. With κ = 0, UCB is the GP mean and exploits; as κ grows, uncertain regions
outscore regions with a high mean. On the reactor, κ = 2 picked the furthest point into
the unknown of the four acquisitions.
items.true: It weights uncertainty more, so it samples more where the GP is unsure: it explores
false: It weights the mean more, so it samples closer to the best point so far: it exploits
Nothing changes, because κ only rescales the acquisition and not its maximizer
It samples where the measurement noise is lowest, because κ divides the noise

items.context: Expected improvement is EI = (μ − f*)Φ(z) + σφ(z). Which part rewards exploration?
items.why:
The first term is large where the mean beats the incumbent, which is exploitation. The
second is large where σ is large, which is exploration. EI carries both in one number.
items.true: The second term, σφ(z): it grows where the GP is uncertain
false: The first term, (μ − f*)Φ(z): it grows where the GP mean is high above the incumbent
Neither term: EI only exploits, which is the reason UCB was invented afterwards
Both terms equally: splitting EI into two terms is only algebra, with no meaning

items.context:
With ξ = 0, probability of improvement keeps picking points just above the best so far.
Why?
items.why:
A point just next to the incumbent beats it with high probability, by a tiny amount. PI
cannot tell that from a likely large gain, so it exploits. EI fixes this by weighting each
improvement by its size.
items.true: It scores only the chance of beating the best, not by how much
false: It uses the GP's standard deviation but ignores the GP's mean completely
It is computed by sampling, so its value is too noisy near the incumbent
Its margin ξ is negative by default, which pulls it toward the incumbent

items.context: Without measurement noise, what is expected improvement at a temperature you already ran?
items.why:
At a measured point σ = 0 and μ is the measured value, at most the incumbent. The
improvement is then zero for sure, so its expected value is zero. EI grows away from the
data.
items.true: Zero: no uncertainty there, and no improvement to expect
false: Its maximum, because the GP is most confident at a measured point
The measured yield itself, because the GP passes through the data
A negative number, which is how the loop avoids repeating experiments

items.context: Why does the worked example use LogExpectedImprovement instead of plain EI?
items.why:
A double-precision number below about 10^-324 is stored as exactly 0. Far from the data EI
is that small, so EI and its slope are both 0 there, and the optimizer that follows the
slope has nowhere to go. LogEI computes log EI directly, with the same maximizer.
items.true: Far from the data, EI and its gradient underflow to zero, and the search stalls
false: Taking the log moves the maximizer, so that the loop explores more than plain EI does
BoTorch can only minimize, so the acquisition has to be turned negative with a log
The log turns EI into a probability that sums to one over all the candidate inputs

items.context: Why does the worked example build the SingleTaskGP with Normalize and Standardize?
items.why:
The kernel's default length scale and the GP's priors assume inputs of order 1 and outputs
of order 1. Temperature in degrees and yields near 0.4 are neither, so BoTorch rescales both
and the defaults become sensible.
items.true: Temperature to [0, 1], yields to mean 0 and standard deviation 1, so the kernel defaults fit
false: Without the two transforms the GP is only an approximation, and with them it becomes exact
The transforms remove the measurement noise from the yields before the GP is fitted
LogExpectedImprovement accepts inputs only between 0 and 1, so the transforms are required

items.context:
The lab gives no gradients, yet optimize_acqf runs gradient-based searches inside the loop.
Why is that fine?
items.why:
Maximizing the acquisition is an optimization over the GP, which is a formula with exact
gradients from automatic differentiation. Only the chosen point is run in the lab.
items.true: It searches the acquisition, a cheap formula from the GP; the experiment runs once per pass
false: BoTorch estimates gradients of the yield itself from the experiments it has already run
It is not fine, and it is the reason BO only works on smooth, noise-free objectives
The gradients come from the Arrhenius formula inside the run_experiment function

items.context:
A team runs BO once on their reactor, reaches the best yield at experiment 6, and reports
"BO finds the optimum in 6 experiments". What is missing?
items.why:
The noise and the random candidates make every run different. The notes report 10 seeds,
random search and two classic optimizers as baselines, the best-so-far curve with its
spread, and the budget counted.
items.true: Several seeds and a baseline: BO is random, and one run proves nothing
false: A larger budget: BO results can only be trusted after many dozens of experiments
A gradient check: the optimum must be confirmed afterwards with L-BFGS-B
Nothing: once the GP is fitted, BO is deterministic and one run is enough

items.context: The lab has four reactors that can run at the same time. Which extension of BO fits?
items.why:
A batch acquisition such as qLogEI scores a set of four points jointly, so the four picks
spread out instead of piling onto the same spot. Four independent loops would each pick
nearly the same experiment.
items.true: Batch BO: choose four experiments at once, with q=4 and a batch acquisition
false: Multi-fidelity BO, because four reactors give four different fidelities
Constrained BO, with one feasibility constraint for each of the reactors
Four independent BO loops, one per reactor, each with its own random seed

items.context: Which of these problems fits Bayesian optimization best?
items.why:
Each evaluation is slow, noisy and has no gradient, and only a few dozen are affordable.
Attia et al. (2020) combined BO with early predictions of battery life for exactly this.
The other two problems have cheap evaluations and gradients.
items.true: Choosing a fast-charging protocol, when each test cycles a battery for days
false: Training an image classifier with millions of weights and cheap exact gradients
Solving a steady-state flowsheet whose Jacobian is analytic and takes milliseconds
Sorting a table of past experiments by their measured yields, highest yield first

items.context:
Data follow y = |x| with a little noise, and there are none for −0.5 < x < 0.5. You fit x
as a straight-line function of y by least squares and ask it which x gives y = 0.75. What
does it answer?
items.why:
Least squares predicts the mean of x given y. Half the points near y = 0.75 sit at
x = −0.75 and half at +0.75, so the prediction lands between them, where there is no data
and no solution. A regression returns one number per input, so it cannot return both.
items.true: About 0, the average of the two answers
false: +0.75, the answer on the branch you happened to picture
−0.75, because the fit is pulled toward negative x
Both −0.75 and +0.75, one per branch

items.context:
Same |x| data. You replace the straight line with a neural network, still trained by
minimizing squared error, to predict x from y. What happens to its answer at y = 0.75?
items.why:
Squared error is minimized by the conditional mean, whatever the model class. With two
branches the mean is between them, so a more flexible regressor reproduces the same wrong
answer. The question, one number for an input with two answers, is the problem.
items.true: It still sits near the mean of the two branches
false: It moves to one of the two branches, since the network can bend
It returns both answers, one per output neuron
It becomes undefined, since the inverse is not a function

items.context:
Which question can a generative model of p(x, y) answer that a regression of y on x
cannot?
items.why:
A model of the joint can be conditioned on any variables. Fixing y and sampling x is an
inverse problem, and the samples include every branch the data support. A regression of y
on x only answers forward.
items.true: Every x consistent with an observed y
false: The expected value of y at a new, unseen x
The gradient of y with respect to each input x
The training error of the fit on the observed data

items.context:
Fitting Gaussian mixtures to the |x| data gives BIC = 543 at K = 1, −697 at K = 2 and
−673 at K = 4. Which number of components does BIC choose?
items.why:
The lowest BIC wins. BIC penalizes parameters, so the extra components at K = 4 raise it
even though they raise the training likelihood. Two components match the two branches.
false: The largest K tried, since likelihood always rises

items.context: How do you condition a fitted Gaussian mixture on known values of some of its variables?
items.why:
Each Gaussian component conditions exactly with the Schur complement formulas. The weights
are updated by the density each component gives the known values, so the result is again
a mixture that can be sampled directly. Rejection sampling (the last option) works in
principle but almost never accepts a sample when the known value is a single point.
items.true: Condition each component exactly, then reweight components by how well they explain the knowns
false: Refit the mixture by EM using only the rows whose known columns match the given values
Keep the single component whose mean lies closest to the known values and sample it alone
Draw samples from the joint and discard every sample that does not match the known values

items.context:
A teammate fitted a Gaussian mixture to rows of (reflux ratio, steam rate, purity) to find
the operating conditions that give a target purity. Now they need the purity predicted for
given operating conditions, and they plan to fit a second mixture for it. What is wrong
with the plan?
items.why:
Which columns are known is an argument to the conditioning step, not a choice made at
fitting time. The one mixture answers the inverse question, the forward question and mixed
ones.
items.true: It is unnecessary; the same mixture conditions on any set of columns
false: Nothing; a mixture can only be conditioned in the direction it was fitted
The second mixture will need twice as many components as the first one
Purity has to be standardized before it can serve as a conditioning variable

items.context: In flow matching, what does the network learn to predict during training?
items.why:
Training pairs a noise sample with a data sample, picks a point on the line between them,
and regresses the network's output onto the line's velocity with mean squared error. No ODE
is solved during training. Predicting added noise is the diffusion formulation, and telling
real from generated is a GAN's discriminator.
items.true: The velocity of a straight line from noise to a data sample
false: The probability density of the data at each point in space
The noise that was added to a data sample at each step
Whether a given sample came from the data or from the generator

items.context:
Every flow-matching training example is a straight line from noise to data. What do the
sampling trajectories, from integrating the learned field, look like?
items.why:
Many training lines pass through a given point at a given time, heading to different data
points. The network learns their average, so paths start slowly and commit to a branch only
partway through. An ODE gives one velocity per point at each time, so no two sampling
particles are ever in the same place at the same time, while the training lines pass
through each other freely.
items.true: Curved, because the field averages the velocities of all lines through a point
false: Straight lines too, because the network was only ever trained on straight lines
Random walks, because each integration step adds a fresh draw of Gaussian noise
Straight, but each one ends at exactly the training point it was paired with

items.context:
You trained a conditional flow-matching model to generate reactor inputs given an output.
Now you need outputs given inputs. What do you do?
items.why:
The condition is an input to the network, fixed when it was trained. Asking a different
question needs a model trained for it. A Gaussian mixture can be conditioned on any columns
afterwards; a conditional flow cannot.
items.true: Train a second model with the inputs as the condition
false: Integrate the same ODE backward from t = 1 to t = 0
Condition the existing model with the Schur complement
Feed the inputs in place of the noise sample

items.context:
You learned p(τ, C_B, dC_B/dτ) for A → B → C in a batch reactor. To find the residence time
that maximizes C_B, what do you condition on?
items.why:
At an interior optimum the derivative is zero, so conditioning on a zero derivative samples
the stationary points. It finds stationary points, not only maxima, so a second condition or
the second-derivative test tells a maximum from a minimum.
items.true: dC_B/dτ = 0
false: d²C_B/dτ² = 0
τ equal to the middle of the sampled range
C_B = 0, the root of the concentration

items.context:
Conditioning a Gaussian mixture on r = 0 gives clusters of Peng-Robinson roots at 0.0440,
0.1273 and 0.8143; numpy.roots gives 0.0348, 0.1280 and 0.8147. What is the right next step?
items.why:
The samples are starting points, one per basin. A few Newton iterations against the true
cubic turn them into the exact roots. The generative model finds every basin at once; the
solver supplies the precision.
items.true: Polish each cluster center with a few Newton steps on the real cubic
false: Report the cluster means, since the surrogate already agrees to two figures
Refit with more and more components until the liquid root finally matches
Discard the liquid root as an artifact of sampling a narrow region

items.context:
Z was sampled uniformly on [0.01, 0.99] and a 12-component mixture was fitted to (Z, r).
The vapor and unstable roots come out within 1%, but the liquid root is 26% high. Which
change fixes it in the course's fit?
items.why:
The liquid root sits in a narrow region where the cubic changes quickly, so the fit there is
sensitive to choices such as K, scaling and seed. Fitting in log Z gives that region more
resolution, and the liquid root comes out at 0.0346 against 0.0348. The paper's own fit
reached 0.035 without it, so this is one fix among several.
items.true: Fit in log Z, which spreads out the small values of Z
false: Use fewer components, so that each one covers more of the data
Condition on r = 0.001 instead of r = 0, to stay clear of the root
Sample Z more coarsely, so that the cubic looks smoother to EM

items.context:
For the same job, how does the data a generative model of p(x, y) needs compare with what a
regression of y on x needs?
items.why:
A regression models how y depends on x. A model of the joint does that and also models the
distribution of x, which is extra work paid for in samples, and density estimation gets
harder fast as the dimension grows. Generated samples are not new data.
items.true: More, because it also has to model how x is distributed
false: Less, because sampling creates new training data
The same, because both see the same rows
Less, because a mixture has fewer parameters than a network

items.context:
You condition a generative model on a value far outside its training data. What do you
get?
items.why:
Nothing in the sampling step checks whether the condition is supported by data. The
notebook asks about the gap in the |x| data and both models answer; the mixture is close to
right only because its straight ellipses extend straight branches.
items.true: Samples, with no warning, shaped by how the model behaves off the data
false: An error, because the condition has zero probability under the model
The single nearest training point, returned exactly and every time
Samples from the unconditional distribution, with the condition ignored

items.context:
A generative model trained on a plant's historian data proposes an optimal operating point.
Which statement is fair?
items.why:
A generative model is a surrogate of the data. Its samples satisfy the learned
distribution, not necessarily the plant, and it learns the plant as it was operated, so the
true optimum may be somewhere the data never went. Tight samples show the surrogate is
confident, not that it is right.
items.true: It solves the surrogate, which only knows the regions the plant has operated in
false: It is optimal for the plant, because every row of the data came from that plant
It is guaranteed feasible, because the operators always kept the plant feasible
It is certified optimal as long as the generated samples are tightly clustered

items.context:
"MatterGen designed a material and the lab measured its property within 20% of the
target." The target bulk modulus was 200 GPa. What does the paper's measurement actually
support?
items.why:
The bulk modulus was estimated from nanoindentation as "up to 169 GPa after four

false: A central estimate within 5% of the target, from four direct measurements
Agreement between DFT and the experiment at 222 GPa, well within the 20%
All four synthesized candidates landing within 20% of their own targets
